Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: Throughout, the essay enters closely and aptly into the meaning, giving particular satisfaction.
Ritual and music receive their names from what is intimately connected with human beings; when put into practice, they bring about good government. How intimately ritual and music concern human beings! If the gentleman can practice them, what difficulty can he have in bringing order to the world? When the Master explained the way of government to Zizhang, he reached this point in answering Zizhang's further question. His meaning was: You have heard that governing depends on understanding ritual and music, but do you recognize that ritual and music are not external to our own persons? People cannot be without words; the difficulty lies in uttering them. To speak and then fulfill one's words is to give them substance in one's own actual conduct and attain □ [illegible]…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
序是即所謂禮焉人不能無行樂之為難行而
樂之有以造於安行之地而得其和是即所謂
樂焉禮樂之切於身如此顧可斯須去之哉君
子者以脩身為本以新民為責知禮之非由外
鑠也致力於禮而著誠去偽必極其序于焉居
南面以出治有德而有位也知樂之非由外至
也致力於樂而反情和志務極其和于焉嚮離
明以答陽有德而有人也由是以序感序言而
人莫不信以和感和行而人莫不從凡被吾之
===
禮教者皆凞凞然於敏德之天一至序之洋溢
凡感吾之樂化者咸皞皞然於同仁之域一至
和之流通諸侯朝而萬物服也庶尹諧而百官
承也天下之平何如哉夫禮樂之本於身而成
大治如此彼鋪筵酌獻之為羽籥鐘鼓之作皆
禮樂之末而已惡足以言政耶嗟夫禮樂之道
大矣自古聖帝明王未有不用禮樂而能成治
者吾夫子有德無位不敢當制作之柄而於禮
樂每拳拳焉其意深矣然子張他日問政一則
punctuated: 序，是即所謂禮焉。人不能無行，樂之為難；行而樂之，有以造於安行之地而得其和，是即所謂樂焉。禮樂之切於身如此，顧可斯須去之哉？君子者，以脩身為本，以新民為責。知禮之非由外鑠也，致力於禮而著誠去偽，必極其序，于焉居南面以出治，有德而有位也；知樂之非由外至也，致力於樂而反情和志，務極其和，于焉嚮離明以答陽，有德而有人也。由是以序感序，言而人莫不信；以和感和，行而人莫不從。凡被吾之禮教者，皆凞凞然於敏德之天，一至序之洋溢；凡感吾之樂化者，咸皞皞然於同仁之域，一至和之流通。諸侯朝而萬物服也，庶尹諧而百官承也，天下之平何如哉？夫禮樂之本於身而成大治如此，彼鋪筵酌獻之為、羽籥鐘鼓之作，皆禮樂之末而已，惡足以言政耶？嗟夫！禮樂之道大矣！自古聖帝明王，未有不用禮樂而能成治者。吾夫子有德無位，不敢當制作之柄，而於禮樂每拳拳焉，其意深矣。然子張他日問政，一則
translation_en:
…order: this is precisely what is called ritual. People cannot avoid acting; what is difficult is to take delight in doing so. When they act with delight, they can reach the point of acting with ease and attain harmony: this is precisely what is called music. Ritual and music are thus intimately bound up with one's own person. Could one dispense with them even for a moment?

The gentleman takes cultivating himself as his foundation and renewing the people as his responsibility. Knowing that ritual is not imposed upon him from outside, he devotes himself to it, manifests sincerity, and eliminates falsity, necessarily bringing its order to perfection. Thereupon he occupies the south-facing seat and brings forth good government: he possesses both virtue and position. Knowing that music does not come from outside, he devotes himself to it, returns to his true feelings, and harmonizes his intentions, striving to perfect its harmony. Thereupon he faces the brightness of the south to respond to yang: he possesses virtue and commands the people's allegiance. Thus, through order he evokes order: when he speaks, everyone trusts him. Through harmony he evokes harmony: when he acts, everyone follows him.

All who receive my instruction in ritual rejoice beneath the heaven of diligent virtue [?], amid the overflowing of consummate order. All who respond to my transforming influence through music are content within a realm of shared benevolence, amid the circulation of consummate harmony. The feudal lords come to court, and all things submit; the various chief officers act in concord, and the hundred officials carry out their duties. How great is the peace of all under Heaven! Such is the way ritual and music, rooted in one's own person, achieve great order. Spreading mats and pouring sacrificial offerings, performing with feathers and pipes, bells and drums—all these are merely the peripheral aspects of ritual and music. How could they suffice for speaking of government?

Ah! Great indeed is the Way of ritual and music! Since antiquity, no sage emperor or enlightened king has ever achieved good government without employing ritual and music. Our Master possessed virtue but held no ruling position. He did not presume to wield the authority to create institutions, yet he was ever deeply devoted to ritual and music. His purpose was profound indeed. Yet when Zizhang asked about government on other occasions, on one occasion…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
告之以無倦以忠一則告之以尊五美屏四惡
與此不同何歟盖爲政之道非一端禮樂則其
本焉爾噫以子張之賢志於爲政徒以少仁而
卒不得與政事之科爲治者當知所務矣
第貳場
論
正心術以立紀綱
張佾
同考試官教諭吳批論場作者詞多浮冗或將
===
陳言平鋪成篇茫無貫串收拾不惟題意無所發明
而昔人論文所謂言之短長聲之高下者亦漫不復
識則亦何所於取而必以是觀士焉哉此作秉其定
見抑揚反復幾千言而皆出自肺腑是足以爲式矣
同考試官教諭陳批闔闢往來無常而脉絡分
明不苟措一語佳作也
同考試官學正周批以天下事勢運量胸中措
之文詞如水湧山出而抑揚豐約自中法度殆素有
所養者
punctuated:
告之以無倦以忠，一則告之以尊五美、屏四惡，與此不同，何歟？盖爲政之道非一端，禮樂則其本焉爾。噫！以子張之賢，志於爲政，徒以少仁，而卒不得與政事之科，爲治者當知所務矣。
第貳場
論
正心術以立紀綱
張佾
同考試官教諭吳批：論場作者，詞多浮冗，或將陳言平鋪成篇，茫無貫串收拾。不惟題意無所發明，而昔人論文所謂言之短長、聲之高下者，亦漫不復識，則亦何所於取，而必以是觀士焉哉？此作秉其定見，抑揚反復幾千言，而皆出自肺腑，是足以爲式矣。
同考試官教諭陳批：闔闢往來無常，而脉絡分明，不苟措一語，佳作也。
同考試官學正周批：以天下事勢運量胸中，措之文詞，如水湧山出，而抑揚豐約自中法度，殆素有所養者。
translation_en:
…he told him to be untiring and loyal; on another occasion he told him to honor the five excellent qualities and banish the four evils. Why do these teachings differ from this one? The way of governing has many aspects, but ritual and music are its foundation. Alas! Worthy as Zizhang was, and intent upon governing, merely because he fell short in benevolence he ultimately could not be numbered among those distinguished in government service. Those who govern should know where to direct their efforts.
Second Session
Discourse
Rectifying the Mind’s Disposition to Establish the Guiding Principles of Government
Zhang Yi
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: Writers in the discourse session mostly employ language that is superficial and redundant. Some spread out stale expressions to make an essay, with no discernible thread connecting its parts or bringing them together. Not only do they fail to illuminate the meaning of the topic; they no longer even recognize what earlier critics of writing called the length and brevity of phrases and the rising and falling of sounds. What, then, is there to value in such writing, that we should insist on using it to assess scholars? This composition maintains a settled viewpoint through thousands of words of emphasis, modulation, and repeated exploration, all issuing from the writer’s innermost heart. It is worthy to serve as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: Its closing and opening, advancing and returning follow no fixed pattern, yet its underlying connections remain clear. Not a single phrase is carelessly placed. This is an excellent composition.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: The writer weighs the affairs and circumstances of the realm within his breast and gives them expression in language like surging water and emerging mountains. Its emphases and modulations, fullness and concision, naturally accord with the rules of composition. Surely he is someone who has long cultivated his capacities.

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭魏批題本正大却難約束是作
者操縱自由而前却顧盼字字詳密且辭氣雄渾敷
暢决非初學可到
考試官教諭林批文思精到筆力健古其視
拾掇補綴者相去遠矣
天下之治有本也善為治者亦惟端其本以運
諸天下而已矣天下之遠民物之繁必有所以
維持經畫之具繁者理而不可棼也遠者舉而
不可廢也夫然後有以布其恤民之實而天下
===
可以言治然不本於人君心術之正則其維持
規畫將必有偏而不舉之處甚則潰散决裂頽
敗委靡而不足以運諸天下其能治軍省賦以
恤天下之民而成治也哉善為治者亦體諸天
而已矣日月星辰行於上昆蟲草木形於下莫
非天道之運也道無不正故其運於外者各得
其正而無爽也人君之心天之心也其術天之
道也固未始有不正也然原於天而具於人動
以天曰道心動以人曰人心人或得以勝天而
punctuated:
考試官教諭魏批：題本正大，却難約束。是作者操縱自由，而前却顧盼，字字詳密，且辭氣雄渾敷暢，决非初學可到。

考試官教諭林批：文思精到，筆力健古，其視拾掇補綴者，相去遠矣。

天下之治有本也，善為治者亦惟端其本，以運諸天下而已矣。天下之遠，民物之繁，必有所以維持經畫之具。繁者理而不可棼也，遠者舉而不可廢也。夫然後有以布其恤民之實，而天下可以言治。然不本於人君心術之正，則其維持規畫將必有偏而不舉之處，甚則潰散决裂，頽敗委靡，而不足以運諸天下。其能治軍省賦，以恤天下之民而成治也哉？善為治者亦體諸天而已矣。日月星辰行於上，昆蟲草木形於下，莫非天道之運也。道無不正，故其運於外者各得其正而無爽也。人君之心，天之心也；其術，天之道也。固未始有不正也。然原於天而具於人，動以天曰道心，動以人曰人心。人或得以勝天，而
translation_en:
Examiner Wei, Instructor, comments: The topic is inherently upright and grand, yet difficult to keep within bounds. This writer handles it freely, advancing and drawing back while attending to what precedes and follows. Every word is carefully considered and precise; moreover, the language is powerful, full, expansive, and fluent. This is certainly beyond the reach of a beginner.

Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: The literary conception is refined and penetrating, and the writing vigorous and antique in manner. It far surpasses the work of those who merely gather scraps and patch them together.

The good governance of All-under-Heaven has a foundation. Those skilled in governing need only set that foundation right and extend its workings throughout the realm. Given the vast extent of All-under-Heaven and the multiplicity of its people and things, there must be means to sustain and order them. What is manifold must be ordered and must not become tangled; what is distant must be attended to and must not be neglected. Only then can genuine care for the people be extended everywhere, and All-under-Heaven be said to be well governed. Yet unless this rests upon the rectitude of the ruler’s mind and its operations, his efforts to sustain and plan will inevitably be partial, leaving some matters unattended. At worst, there will be disintegration and rupture, decline and enfeeblement, making it impossible to extend his governing efforts throughout the realm. How could he then put the military in order and reduce taxation, caring for the people of All-under-Heaven and achieving good governance?

Those skilled in governing need only take Heaven as their model. The sun, moon, and stars move above; insects, grasses, and trees take form below: all are workings of the Way of Heaven. Nothing in that Way is other than correct; thus, in its outward workings, everything attains its proper order without deviation. The ruler’s mind is Heaven’s mind; its operations are Heaven’s Way. Originally, there is indeed nothing in them that is not correct. Yet what originates in Heaven is embodied in human beings: when its movement proceeds from Heaven, it is called the mind of the Way; when its movement proceeds from the human, it is called the human mind. The human may come to prevail over Heaven, and …

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
其術始有不得其正者正則公公則溥不正則
私私則偏故君心天下之本而其術不可以不
正也五方風氣異宜暴悍之徒横戾乎其間其
勢易渙而不属强者弱者狡而黠者愚者詐者
縱横雜揉相侵越而不得其分其勢易紛而不
理茍非法以制之則合渙解紛卒無其道雖欲
恤民而澤不下究民焉所恃而安乎是故紀綱
不可以不立也其所以為之者心也心之所嚮
好惡取舍出於私人亦得以其私所好惡者干
===
焉巧者辯者奸而佞者日變其情以投吾隙柄
移於人人而捉之也無綱法窳於紛更而肅之
也無紀天下其曷由治哉盖徒法不能以自行
而欲正夫法不本諸心術之正不可也是必稽
之往昔驗之當今考之天人之際慮之熟而辨
之精異端邪說舉不足以惑吾聽趨向端矣存
養之也密而體驗擴充之也至聲色貨利遊畋
之欲舉不得以萌于心其有好也好必出於大
理之公人不得以其私好者干我也非惟人不
punctuated: 其術始有不得其正者。正則公，公則溥；不正則私，私則偏。故君心，天下之本，而其術不可以不正也。五方風氣異宜，暴悍之徒横戾乎其間，其勢易渙而不属。强者、弱者、狡而黠者、愚者、詐者，縱横雜揉，相侵越而不得其分，其勢易紛而不理。茍非法以制之，則合渙解紛，卒無其道。雖欲恤民，而澤不下究，民焉所恃而安乎？是故紀綱不可以不立也。其所以為之者，心也。心之所嚮，好惡取舍出於私，人亦得以其私所好惡者干焉。巧者、辯者、奸而佞者，日變其情以投吾隙。柄移於人，人而捉之也無綱；法窳於紛更，而肅之也無紀。天下其曷由治哉？盖徒法不能以自行，而欲正夫法，不本諸心術之正，不可也。是必稽之往昔，驗之當今，考之天人之際，慮之熟而辨之精，異端邪說舉不足以惑吾聽，趨向端矣。存養之也密，而體驗擴充之也至，聲色貨利遊畋之欲舉不得以萌于心。其有好也，好必出於大理之公，人不得以其私好者干我也。非惟人不
translation_en:
…only then do his methods begin to depart from what is correct. Correctness leads to impartiality, and impartiality to universal reach; incorrectness leads to selfishness, and selfishness to partiality. Thus the ruler’s heart is the foundation of all under Heaven, and his methods must be correct. Customs and dispositions differ throughout the five regions, and violent, fierce men act lawlessly among them; such circumstances readily lead to dispersal and a loss of cohesion. The strong, the weak, the cunning and crafty, the foolish, and the deceitful mingle in every direction, encroaching upon one another and failing to keep to their proper stations. Such circumstances readily lead to confusion and disorder. Unless laws restrain them, there is ultimately no way to unite what is dispersed and resolve what is confused. Even if the ruler wishes to care for the people, his beneficence does not reach down to them. Upon what, then, can the people rely for security? Thus the governing framework and disciplinary order must be established.

What puts these into effect is the heart. If the heart’s inclinations—its likes and dislikes, its choices and rejections—arise from selfishness, others too can intrude with their own private likes and dislikes. The artful, the eloquent, the treacherous and flattering daily change their outward dispositions to exploit my vulnerabilities. Authority passes into others’ hands, and there is no governing framework by which to grasp it [?]; laws deteriorate through incessant alteration, and there is no disciplinary order by which to enforce them. How, then, can all under Heaven be governed? Laws alone cannot put themselves into effect. To seek to rectify the laws without grounding them in the correctness of one’s heart and intentions is impossible.

One must therefore investigate the past, test matters against the present, examine the relationship between Heaven and humanity, reflect thoroughly, and discriminate precisely. When heterodox doctrines and perverse teachings are altogether incapable of confusing what I hear, my direction will be correct. If I preserve and nurture this with close attention, and fully realize it in experience and extend it, desires for music and sensual beauty, wealth and profit, recreation and hunting will find no opportunity to sprout in my heart. Whenever I have a liking, it must arise from the impartiality of the great principle, so that others cannot intrude upon me with their private preferences. Not only do others not…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
作而干吾亦不得而與吾私焉其於惡也亦然
由是朝廷之上予奪慶讓咸以天下之公左右
便嬖雖欲肆其巧佞以售其奸吾且以天下之
公而黜罰之矣而况敢貳吾柄乎哉由是以兆
民責司徒以百工責司空則凡優其財力時其
征賦皆舉之矣以大禮責宗伯以軍旅責司馬
以刑罰責司寇則凡事神育才治軍衞民皆舉
之矣強不得以凌弱詐不得以罔愚奸暴不得
以肆侮經營區畫條分而畛别絲牽而繩聯親
===
而不相越也辨而無或暌也且又各以其属而
統諸大者尊者上振而下肅内舉而外張自朝
廷而百官而萬民無非承一人好惡之公而莫
敢或私焉而天下固運諸掌矣盖人之心其始
得於天也極天下之物而無乎不包故其用也
盡萬物之性而無一或謬正如天之化成萬物
而莫有外乎道者也人君紀綱天下以致其恤
民之實者豈有求於心之外哉抑斯言也朱
子之所以告其君也當其時□□以債名士爲私
punctuated: 作而干，吾亦不得而與吾私焉。其於惡也亦然。由是朝廷之上，予奪慶讓，咸以天下之公。左右便嬖雖欲肆其巧佞以售其奸，吾且以天下之公而黜罰之矣，而况敢貳吾柄乎哉？由是以兆民責司徒，以百工責司空，則凡優其財力、時其征賦，皆舉之矣。以大禮責宗伯，以軍旅責司馬，以刑罰責司寇，則凡事神育才、治軍衞民，皆舉之矣。強不得以凌弱，詐不得以罔愚，奸暴不得以肆侮。經營區畫，條分而畛别，絲牽而繩聯，親而不相越也，辨而無或暌也。且又各以其属而統諸大者、尊者，上振而下肅，内舉而外張。自朝廷而百官而萬民，無非承一人好惡之公，而莫敢或私焉，而天下固運諸掌矣。盖人之心，其始得於天也，極天下之物而無乎不包；故其用也，盡萬物之性而無一或謬。正如天之化成萬物，而莫有外乎道者也。人君紀綱天下，以致其恤民之實者，豈有求於心之外哉？抑斯言也，朱子之所以告其君也。當其時，□□以債名士爲私
translation_en:
…come forward to interfere, nor could I indulge my own partiality in dealing with them [?]. The same applies to dislikes. Thus, at court, grants and withdrawals, rewards and reprimands would all accord with impartial standards shared by all under Heaven. Even if intimate attendants and favorites wished to give free rein to their cunning flattery and advance their treacherous designs, I would dismiss and punish them according to those impartial standards. How, then, would they dare to divide my authority?

Accordingly, the Minister of Education would be held responsible for the multitudes, and the Minister of Works for the various artisans; all measures to replenish the people's resources and strength and to levy taxes and services at the proper times would be carried out. The Minister of Rites would be held responsible for the great ceremonies, the Minister of War for military affairs, and the Minister of Justice for punishments; all matters of serving the spirits, nurturing talent, ordering the army, and protecting the people would be accomplished. The strong could not oppress the weak, the deceitful could not hoodwink the simple, and the treacherous and violent could not freely perpetrate their outrages. Administrative arrangements and divisions would be clearly differentiated, with distinct boundaries, yet linked like threads drawn together and cords joined. They would be closely connected without encroaching upon one another, distinct without becoming estranged.

Moreover, each would be grouped with its subordinate offices under those of greater scope and higher rank. When those above acted vigorously, those below would be disciplined; when affairs were set in motion at the center, their effects would extend outward. From the court to the hundred officials and the myriad people, all would uphold the impartiality of the sovereign's likes and dislikes, and none would dare pursue private interests. The realm could then indeed be turned about in the palm of one's hand.

For the human mind, as originally received from Heaven, embraces everything in the world, leaving nothing outside it. Thus, in its operation, it fully realizes the nature of all things without a single error. This is precisely like Heaven's transforming and bringing all things to completion, with none lying outside the Way. When the ruler establishes the governing order of the realm so as to give practical effect to his concern for the people, how could he seek anything outside the mind?

These words were what Master Zhu used to admonish his ruler. At that time, □□ used debts to make eminent scholars his private adherents [?] …

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
後賦役繁興而民日困紀綱之不立至是盖亦
甚矣朱子以格心之學拳拳焉欲以正君德而
飭天下之治乃卒不見用焉何哉顧其言垂於
今猶足以爲百世法舍是而圖治未有能行者
也然心術邪正必學焉然後能擇擇焉然後能
守舜所謂惟精惟一者是也君天下者欲正其
心術必自明學術始
表
擬宋太祖親賛孔顔文臣謝表建隆二年
===
羅星
同考試官教諭鄭批以孔顔事實織組成篇且
聲律可誦噫子其負楚士之重名者乎
考試官教諭魏批表多警句讀之令人起敬
考試官教諭林批爾雅典重表必如此乃佳
某年某月某日具官臣等欽蒙
聖恩親賛孔顔者昌言賛聖兆啓虞廷本傳稽
賢事隆漢史光昭闕里典出
清朝時祀聿崇夙荷無涯之寵
punctuated:
後，賦役繁興，而民日困，紀綱之不立，至是盖亦甚矣。朱子以格心之學拳拳焉，欲以正君德而飭天下之治，乃卒不見用焉，何哉？顧其言垂於今，猶足以爲百世法，舍是而圖治，未有能行者也。然心術邪正，必學焉然後能擇，擇焉然後能守，舜所謂「惟精惟一」者是也。君天下者欲正其心術，必自明學術始。
表
擬宋太祖親賛孔顔文臣謝表，建隆二年。
羅星
同考試官教諭鄭批：「以孔顔事實織組成篇，且聲律可誦。噫！子其負楚士之重名者乎！」
考試官教諭魏批：「表多警句，讀之令人起敬。」
考試官教諭林批：「爾雅典重，表必如此乃佳。」
某年某月某日，具官臣等欽蒙聖恩親賛孔顔者。昌言賛聖，兆啓虞廷；本傳稽賢，事隆漢史。光昭闕里，典出清朝。時祀聿崇，夙荷無涯之寵。
translation_en:
… thereafter, taxes and labor services multiplied, and the people grew poorer by the day. The failure to establish governing order had indeed reached an extreme. Master Zhu earnestly advocated the learning that rectifies the ruler’s mind, hoping thereby to correct the ruler’s virtue and bring good order to the realm. Why, then, was he ultimately never employed? Yet his words, handed down to the present, remain sufficient to serve as a model for a hundred generations. No one who abandons this approach in seeking good government has ever succeeded. To distinguish right from wrong in the inclinations of the mind, however, one must first study before one can choose, and choose before one can hold fast. This is what Shun meant by “Be discerning; be single-minded.” A ruler of the realm who wishes to rectify his mind’s inclinations must begin by clarifying the teachings he follows.
Memorial
A memorial of thanks by the civil officials, composed as if on the occasion when Emperor Taizu of the Song personally wrote eulogies of Kongzi and Yan Hui, in the second year of Jianlong [961].
By Luo Xing.
Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: “He has woven the deeds of Kongzi and Yan Hui into a composition whose rhythms also lend themselves to recitation. Ah! Are you perhaps one who will uphold the great reputation of the scholars of Chu?”
Examiner Wei, Instructor, comments: “The memorial contains many striking phrases. Reading it inspires respect.”
Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: “Refined, classical, and dignified: a memorial must be like this to be excellent.”
On a certain day of a certain month in a certain year, we, your servants holding the designated offices, have reverently received Your Majesty’s gracious favor in personally composing eulogies of Kongzi and Yan Hui.
Praising the sage with noble words had its beginnings at the court of Shun; examining the worthy through their biographies became an honored undertaking in the histories of the Han. Radiance now shines upon Queli, and this ceremonial act issues from your enlightened court. Seasonal sacrifices have been exalted; long have they received your boundless favor…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
奎章是錫式垂不朽之名感無任于再三
恩復覃乎七十臣等誠懽誠忭稽首頓首
上言伏以夫子不可及也緬懷鑽仰之無階
顏氏其庶幾乎竊擬俯焉而有據高天厚
地屹爲萬世之宗和風慶雲夐出疇人之
右燕居琴瑟陋巷簞瓢間譽聖而更疑或
推賢而竟詆師生相信授受一時忘食忘
憂不知老之將至亦趨亦步雖欲從之末
由絃歌不輟於在陳雅頌頓釐於反魯安
===
其所遇有惟與爾之稱悅而不疑啟非助
我之嘆典刑具在影響終遐緒論家藏末
學日盛入耳出口疇能悟一貫之傳買櫝
還珠亦鮮窺十知之奧漢祖太牢一祀禮
則倉皇唐宗廟貌肇新制仍疎畧容狥名
而昧實僭以僞而仇真遂令二帝謨謀猶
寓簡編之陳蹟與夫四代禮樂徒爲問答
之空言粤自生民以來惟賜也能道其盛
抑昔吾友從事非參乎孰與於斯盖談海
punctuated: 奎章是錫，式垂不朽之名。感無任于再三，恩復覃乎七十。臣等誠懽誠忭，稽首頓首上言：伏以夫子不可及也，緬懷鑽仰之無階；顏氏其庶幾乎，竊擬俯焉而有據。高天厚地，屹爲萬世之宗；和風慶雲，夐出疇人之右。燕居琴瑟，陋巷簞瓢。間譽聖而更疑，或推賢而竟詆。師生相信，授受一時。忘食忘憂，不知老之將至；亦趨亦步，雖欲從之末由。絃歌不輟於在陳，雅頌頓釐於反魯。安其所遇，有惟與爾之稱；悅而不疑，啟非助我之嘆。典刑具在，影響終遐。緒論家藏，末學日盛。入耳出口，疇能悟一貫之傳？買櫝還珠，亦鮮窺十知之奧。漢祖太牢一祀，禮則倉皇；唐宗廟貌肇新，制仍疎畧。容狥名而昧實，僭以僞而仇真。遂令二帝謨謀，猶寓簡編之陳蹟；與夫四代禮樂，徒爲問答之空言。粤自生民以來，惟賜也能道其盛；抑昔吾友從事，非參乎孰與於斯？盖談海
translation_en:
…Your Majesty has bestowed imperial compositions, thereby conferring imperishable renown. Our gratitude for these repeated favors knows no bounds; your grace extends also to the seventy disciples. We, your servants, sincerely rejoice and exult; bowing our heads to the ground, we respectfully submit:
We humbly consider that the Master cannot be equaled: yearning toward him, we have no stair by which to probe his teaching and look up to him. Yet Yan Hui perhaps came close; we venture to take him as a more accessible example for which there is firm warrant [?]. Like lofty Heaven and the deep Earth, the Master stands as the exemplar of ten thousand generations; like a gentle breeze and auspicious clouds, Yan Hui rises far above ordinary men. In quiet retirement there were zithers; in a narrow lane, a basket of rice and a gourd of water. Some praised the sage yet still doubted him; others commended the worthy yet ultimately disparaged him. Teacher and pupil trusted one another, transmitting and receiving the teaching in their own time. The one forgot food and sorrow, unaware that old age was approaching; the other followed at a walk and at a run, yet, though he wished to follow further, found no way to do so. Singing to strings did not cease during the sojourn in Chen; the Greater and Lesser Odes were duly set in order upon the return to Lu. Content with whatever circumstances he encountered, Yan Hui earned the commendation, “Only you and I can do this.” Delighting in the teaching without questioning it, he prompted the remark, “He is no help to me.”
Their exemplary patterns remain intact, yet their living presence and voices are distant indeed. Their surviving teachings are treasured in every household, while superficial learning increases daily. When words merely enter the ear and leave the mouth, who can grasp the transmitted teaching of the single thread running through all? Buying the casket and returning the pearl, few glimpse the profundity of understanding ten things upon hearing one. The Han founder once offered the full sacrifice of ox, sheep, and pig, but the ceremony was hurried; a Tang emperor renewed the temple buildings, but the arrangements remained inadequate. Thus there was room to pursue reputation while remaining blind to substance, and presumptuously to use falsehood to oppose truth. Consequently, the counsels of the Two Emperors remained merely ancient traces preserved in books, while the rites and music of the Four Dynasties became only empty words exchanged in questions and answers.
Since human beings first existed, only Ci could express the full greatness of the Master. And, among those who once worked alongside him as friends, who but Shen could have participated in this? For to speak of the sea…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
嶽每難為言譬飲江河僅止知足措片詞
之未易矧兩賛之兼工茲盖伏遇
〇〇〇〇
天挺
真人民歸
義主
沉幾先物
至誠感神懋文王之德之純似周公之才
之美
===
身親軍旅寧忘展卷之勤洞開
殿門大悟正心之學釋兵權僅憑杯酒購竒
書不吝千金宰相用以書生宿儒處之翰
苑遂留情於爼豆廼稅
駕於宫墻憤悱聖賢蒐羅幽賾望儼然而莫
即諒今也之則亡謂孔子集未集之大成
功高千古謂顏子發不發之精蘊名冠四
科道渴潜心教明指掌顧幽光而未闡惜
舊典其猶虧乃啓
punctuated:
嶽，每難為言；譬飲江河，僅止知足。措片詞之未易，矧兩賛之兼工！茲盖伏遇〇〇〇〇天挺真人，民歸義主，沉幾先物，至誠感神。懋文王之德之純，似周公之才之美。

身親軍旅，寧忘展卷之勤？洞開殿門，大悟正心之學。釋兵權，僅憑杯酒；購竒書，不吝千金。宰相用以書生，宿儒處之翰苑。遂留情於爼豆，廼稅駕於宫墻。憤悱聖賢，蒐羅幽賾。望儼然而莫即，諒今也之則亡。謂孔子集未集之大成，功高千古；謂顏子發不發之精蘊，名冠四科。道渴潜心，教明指掌。顧幽光而未闡，惜舊典其猶虧，乃啓
translation_en:
…mountains: it is always difficult to put their grandeur into words. It is like drinking from the great rivers: one can only drink one's fill. Even composing a few words is no easy matter; how much harder to make both eulogies excellent! Now we have humbly encountered 〇〇〇〇 a true sovereign raised up by Heaven, a righteous ruler to whom the people turn. His profound discernment anticipates events; his perfect sincerity moves the spirits. He cultivates the purity of King Wen's virtue and resembles the Duke of Zhou in the excellence of his talents.

Though personally engaged in military campaigns, how could he forget his diligent reading? He opened wide the palace gates and thoroughly comprehended the learning of rectifying the mind. With merely a cup of wine he secured the relinquishment of military command; to purchase rare books he begrudged not a thousand pieces of gold. He employed scholars as grand councilors and placed venerable Confucian scholars in the Hanlin Academy. Thus he turned his attention to the sacrificial vessels and halted his carriage at the walls of the Sage's temple. Eager to understand and articulate the teachings of the sages and worthies, he searched out their hidden profundities. He gazed upon that august presence but could not approach it, knowing that now the Sage was indeed no more. He declared that Confucius brought together into a great synthesis what had never before been united, his achievement surpassing all ages; and that Master Yan revealed subtle truths never before disclosed, his renown foremost among the four branches of learning. Thirsting for the Way, he devoted his mind to it [?]; the teaching was as clear as something pointed out in his palm. Yet, seeing that their hidden radiance had not been fully revealed, and regretting that the old ceremonial provisions remained deficient, he thereupon initiated…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
宸裁親摛
神翰攄胸中之藻思渙天下之至文點竄不
加揄揚殆盡想魯論半部次第施行倣鄉
黨一篇分明畫出雖後聖之復作亦斯言
之必從也臣等逵羽鵷班濫竽儒列志存
師孔學竊晞顔遲回於意必固我之間奮
迅於視聽言動之頃幸逢
盛典雅愜初懷知一朝之塞雖窮匪窮信萬禩
之長不壽亦壽事固有期而益顯道實待
===
人而後行傳心之敎彌章在天之靈亦慰
臣工朗誦朝野忻聞反己而求誓終身取
法于上因言以獻願
奕葉允執厥中五星永聚于奎躔人文與天
文爭耀六籍大明於日出
國脉與道脉同春臣等無任瞻
天仰
聖激切屛營之至謹奉
表稱
punctuated:
宸裁，親摛神翰，攄胸中之藻思，渙天下之至文。點竄不加，揄揚殆盡。想《魯論》半部，次第施行；倣《鄉黨》一篇，分明畫出。雖後聖之復作，亦斯言之必從也。
臣等逵羽鵷班，濫竽儒列，志存師孔，學竊晞顔。遲回於意必固我之間，奮迅於視聽言動之頃。幸逢盛典，雅愜初懷。知一朝之塞，雖窮匪窮；信萬禩之長，不壽亦壽。事固有期而益顯，道實待人而後行。傳心之敎彌章，在天之靈亦慰。臣工朗誦，朝野忻聞。反己而求，誓終身取法于上；因言以獻，願奕葉允執厥中。五星永聚于奎躔，人文與天文爭耀；六籍大明於日出，國脉與道脉同春。臣等無任瞻天仰聖、激切屛營之至，謹奉表稱
translation_en:
…the imperial judgment. Your Majesty personally wielded the imperial brush, expressing the elegant conceptions within your breast and promulgating writing of supreme excellence throughout the realm. No revision was needed; its praise was almost exhaustive. We imagine half of the Analects being put into practice, step by step, and its chapter “The Village Community” (Xiangdang) being followed and vividly depicted. Even if a later sage should arise, he would assuredly follow these words.
We, your servants, occupy the ranks of court officials [?], unworthily numbered among the scholars. Our ambition is to take Confucius as our teacher; in learning, we privately aspire to emulate Yan Hui. We linger amid conjecture, insistence, obstinacy, and self-centeredness, yet strive vigorously in seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting. Fortunately encountering this grand observance, we find our original aspirations fully satisfied. We know that an obstruction lasting but a day, though a hardship, is no true hardship; we trust that endurance through ten thousand years is longevity, even without a long life. An undertaking becomes more illustrious when its time arrives; the Way indeed awaits someone to put it into practice. The teaching that transmits the heart becomes ever clearer, and the spirits in Heaven are also consoled. Your officials recite it aloud; court and countryside rejoice to hear it. Turning inward to examine ourselves, we vow throughout our lives to take our model from above. Offering these words, we pray that successive generations may faithfully hold fast to the Mean. May the five planets forever gather in the celestial lodge Kui, and human culture vie in brilliance with the patterns of Heaven; may the Six Classics shine brightly at sunrise, and the vitality of the state and the vitality of the Way flourish together in perpetual spring. We, your servants, look up to Heaven and revere Your Sagely Majesty, overcome with fervent emotion and reverent trepidation. We respectfully present this memorial to express…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
謝以
聞
第參塲
策
第一問
羅星
同考試官教諭鄭批尊德性道問學此聖賢心
學工夫自古帝王及我
聖祖神宗之所以授受講說者皆是物也著之簡策實為昭明諸士子言
之而或遺焉豈習矣而未之察邪抑亦聖學淵深而
未易以言論形容之邪此篇條答詳明鋪敘嚴整足
以發我
列聖獨得之妙於一日之間非仰窺
聖心有在者不能末復歸之主敬一語尤為有見錄之可以為
當宁獻矣
考試官教諭魏批讀子前塲已諒其不凡及
觀五策尤見學識此篇鋪張我
祖宗心學之大鑿鑿無遺又能掲出敬天恤民為
punctuated:
謝以聞。
第參塲，策，第一問。羅星。
同考試官教諭鄭批：「尊德性，道問學，此聖賢心學工夫。自古帝王及我聖祖神宗之所以授受講說者，皆是物也。著之簡策，實為昭明。諸士子言之而或遺焉，豈習矣而未之察邪？抑亦聖學淵深，而未易以言論形容之邪？此篇條答詳明，鋪敘嚴整，足以發我列聖獨得之妙於一日之間。非仰窺聖心有在者不能。末復歸之主敬一語，尤為有見。錄之，可以為當宁獻矣。」
考試官教諭魏批：「讀子前塲，已諒其不凡；及觀五策，尤見學識。此篇鋪張我祖宗心學之大，鑿鑿無遺，又能掲出敬天恤民為
translation_en:
…thanks, respectfully submitted for imperial hearing.

Third Session: Policy Essays, Question One. Luo Xing.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: “Honoring the moral nature and pursuing inquiry and learning: these are the practices of the learning of the mind cultivated by sages and worthies. What emperors and kings since antiquity, together with our sagely progenitor and divine ancestors, have transmitted, received, discussed, and expounded is all this same teaching. Set down in written records, it is indeed perfectly clear. Yet when examination candidates discuss it, some leave things out. Is this because they have grown accustomed to it without examining it? Or is the learning of the sages so profound that it cannot readily be expressed in words? This essay answers point by point, thoroughly and clearly, with a rigorously ordered exposition. It succeeds, within a single day, in bringing to light the subtleties uniquely grasped by our successive sage emperors. Only someone who has gained some insight into the imperial mind could accomplish this. Its conclusion returns once more to the single phrase ‘making reverent attentiveness the guiding principle,’ showing particular discernment. Recorded here, it may be presented to the reigning emperor.”

Comment by Examiner Wei, Instructor: “On reading your work from the preceding sessions, I already recognized its exceptional quality; upon examining your five policy essays, I saw your learning and discernment still more clearly. This essay fully expounds the greatness of our imperial ancestors’ learning of the mind, with firm substantiation and no omissions. It also succeeds in identifying revering Heaven and caring for the people as …

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
其必積學而知要者乎擢居首選允愜輿情
考試官敎諭林批事核而實辭富不華能誦
列聖心學之詳居常必思報創業垂統覆載之恩歟
帝王學術之先務豈有他哉正心以立其
本窮理以盡其要而已蓋尊德性所以正
心而道問學所以窮理也然欲務其學而
以正心為本欲正其心而以窮理為要則
凡所以施為舉措必皆不失其心之權度
而為治者之能事畢矣此自古帝王心學
===
之急務皆我
祖宗列聖所優為也執事發策下詢首及於此
敢不敬對於萬一乎何以言之人君一身
為天下之主天命去留之所繫民情安危
之所關而心也者又萬化之所從以出也
是以古昔帝王莫不以心學為先務若堯
舜禹湯文武之為君曰人心惟危道心惟
微惟精惟一允執厥中而已顧諟明命緝
煕敬止建其有極而已是雖無事於講習
punctuated:
其必積學而知要者乎？擢居首選，允愜輿情。

考試官敎諭林批：事核而實，辭富不華。能誦列聖心學之詳，居常必思報創業垂統覆載之恩歟！

帝王學術之先務，豈有他哉？正心以立其本，窮理以盡其要而已。蓋尊德性所以正心，而道問學所以窮理也。然欲務其學，而以正心為本；欲正其心，而以窮理為要，則凡所以施為舉措，必皆不失其心之權度，而為治者之能事畢矣。此自古帝王心學之急務，皆我祖宗列聖所優為也。執事發策下詢，首及於此，敢不敬對於萬一乎？何以言之？人君一身，為天下之主，天命去留之所繫，民情安危之所關，而心也者，又萬化之所從以出也。是以古昔帝王，莫不以心學為先務。若堯舜禹湯文武之為君，曰「人心惟危，道心惟微，惟精惟一，允執厥中」而已；「顧諟明命」、「緝煕敬止」、「建其有極」而已。是雖無事於講習
translation_en:
…Surely he must be one who has accumulated learning and grasped its essentials! Elevating him to first place truly accords with general opinion.

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: His treatment of affairs is well founded and substantial; his language is rich without being ornate. Able to recount in detail the learning of the mind practiced by our sage emperors, he must surely reflect continually on repaying their beneficence in founding the dynasty, transmitting its succession, and sheltering and sustaining all like Heaven and Earth!

Could the foremost task in the learning of emperors and kings be anything else? It is simply to rectify the mind so as to establish its foundation, and to investigate principle so as to comprehend its essentials fully. For honoring one's moral nature is the means of rectifying the mind, while pursuing inquiry and learning is the means of investigating principle. If, in pursuing learning, one takes rectification of the mind as the foundation, and, in seeking to rectify the mind, one takes investigation of principle as the essential task, then every action and undertaking will accord with the mind's standards of judgment, and all that a ruler can accomplish will be fulfilled. These urgent tasks in the learning of the mind practiced by emperors and kings since antiquity are all things in which our dynastic ancestors and sage emperors have excelled. You, honored examiners, have issued policy questions to inquire of us below, addressing this subject first. How could I dare not respectfully offer an answer, however small a portion of it I can encompass?

How may this be explained? The ruler, in his own person, is lord of all under Heaven. On him depends whether Heaven's Mandate departs or remains; with him are bound up the people's security and peril. The mind, moreover, is the source from which all transforming influences proceed. Thus the emperors and kings of antiquity invariably made the learning of the mind their foremost task. As rulers, Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu held simply to these words: “The human mind is precarious; the mind of the Way is subtle. Be discerning, be single-minded, and sincerely hold fast to the mean.” They did no more than “keep constantly in view Heaven's bright Mandate,” “continue in radiant virtue, abiding in reverence,” and “establish the supreme standard.” Although this involved no formal exposition and study…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
而學在其中宜其治道之隆巍乎不可尚
焉自是以降秦不足言而漢而唐而宋其
間英君誼辟亦非不願治也然或不事詩
書或内多慚德或詞藻末務焉良以心有
未純而學無足取治不古若有由然哉洪
惟我
太祖高皇帝嘗作觀心亭命宋濂爲之記而復
示以返觀却聽上契冲漠之言其有事方
丘問宋濂以心之不寧而嘉納其養心寡
===
欲心清身泰之奏
太宗文皇帝於學士解縉進呈大學正心之講
義而有明鏡止水之諭
英宗睿皇帝於處士吳與弼啓沃誠意正心之
理學而有
寵賚進擢之加寧非尊德性以爲之本乎
太祖高皇帝觀大學衍義鼂錯之言而知其濫
刑黷兵爲可戒聞學士朱善周易家人之
講而悟其齊家治國無二理
punctuated:
而學在其中，宜其治道之隆，巍乎不可尚焉。自是以降，秦不足言，而漢而唐而宋，其間英君誼辟，亦非不願治也。然或不事詩書，或内多慚德，或詞藻末務焉。良以心有未純，而學無足取，治不古若，有由然哉！洪惟我太祖高皇帝嘗作觀心亭，命宋濂爲之記，而復示以返觀却聽、上契冲漠之言。其有事方丘，問宋濂以心之不寧，而嘉納其養心寡欲、心清身泰之奏。太宗文皇帝於學士解縉進呈《大學》正心之講義，而有明鏡止水之諭。英宗睿皇帝於處士吳與弼啓沃誠意正心之理學，而有寵賚進擢之加。寧非尊德性以爲之本乎？
太祖高皇帝觀《大學衍義》鼂錯之言，而知其濫刑黷兵爲可戒；聞學士朱善《周易》家人之講，而悟其齊家治國無二理。
translation_en:
…yet learning was contained therein. No wonder their way of governing attained such heights that nothing could surpass it. Thereafter, leaving aside Qin as unworthy of discussion, among the Han, Tang, and Song there were enlightened rulers and righteous sovereigns who certainly wished for good government. Yet some neglected the Odes and Documents, some inwardly harbored much shameful conduct, and some devoted themselves to the secondary pursuit of literary embellishment. Indeed, because their minds were not wholly pure and their learning offered little of worth, there was good reason why their government fell short of antiquity!
We reverently consider how our Emperor Taizu Gao once built the Pavilion for Contemplating the Mind and ordered Song Lian to compose an account of it. He further instructed him with words about turning one's vision inward and withdrawing one's hearing, thereby attaining accord with the ultimate stillness and emptiness. When he offered sacrifice at the Square Mound, he asked Song Lian why his mind was unsettled and graciously accepted his memorial on nurturing the mind by diminishing desires, so that the mind would be clear and the person at peace. When Academician Xie Jin presented a lecture exposition on rectifying the mind in the Great Learning, Emperor Taizong Wen issued an instruction invoking a bright mirror and still water. When the scholar without office Wu Yubi expounded for Emperor Yingzong Rui the learning of principle concerning making the intentions sincere and rectifying the mind, the emperor bestowed generous rewards and offered him advancement to office. Was this not to make honoring one's moral nature the foundation?
Emperor Taizu Gao read the words of Chao Cuo in the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning and recognized Chao's excessive use of punishments and reckless resort to arms as warnings. Hearing Academician Zhu Shan's exposition of the Family hexagram in the Changes of Zhou, he understood that ordering the family and governing the state follow one and the same principle.…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
太宗文皇帝覽楊士奇進呈講義特信其克明
峻德一章已具一部大學之道
宣宗章皇帝覽歐陽脩夢卜求賢之說深知其
恭默思道且嘆君臣相遇之難寧非道問
學以為之要乎是則尊德性固所以為道
問學之本而道問學實所以為尊德性之
要二者更互為用誠亦不可以偏廢焉揆
諸精一執中之傳千載同符
列聖相承永為家法其所以垂萬世無疆之休
===
者豈偶然之故耶噫帝王之學與韋布不
同苟徒區區於記誦詞章之末則非所以
窮理而立天下之本矣然是學也其所以
成始而成終者又有在於敬焉必思上帝
之臨汝則此心凛凛不敢怠也必視小民
之如傷則此心皇皇不敢肆也此皆帝王
相傳之大法
祖宗垂裕之要道而不可忽焉者方今
天子在上聰明睿知敬天恤民克嗣前烈而
punctuated:
太宗文皇帝覽楊士奇進呈講義，特信其克明峻德一章已具一部大學之道。宣宗章皇帝覽歐陽脩夢卜求賢之說，深知其恭默思道，且嘆君臣相遇之難，寧非道問學以為之要乎？是則尊德性固所以為道問學之本，而道問學實所以為尊德性之要，二者更互為用，誠亦不可以偏廢焉。揆諸精一執中之傳，千載同符。列聖相承，永為家法，其所以垂萬世無疆之休者，豈偶然之故耶？

噫！帝王之學與韋布不同，苟徒區區於記誦詞章之末，則非所以窮理而立天下之本矣。然是學也，其所以成始而成終者，又有在於敬焉。必思上帝之臨汝，則此心凛凛不敢怠也；必視小民之如傷，則此心皇皇不敢肆也。此皆帝王相傳之大法，祖宗垂裕之要道，而不可忽焉者。

方今天子在上，聰明睿知，敬天恤民，克嗣前烈，而
translation_en:
Emperor Wen (Taizong), on reading the lecture explanations submitted by Yang Shiqi, was particularly convinced that the chapter on “being able to manifest lofty virtue” already contained the Way of the entire Great Learning. Emperor Zhang (Xuanzong), on reading Ouyang Xiu’s discussion of seeking worthy men through dreams and divination, deeply understood the meaning of reverently contemplating the Way in silence, and also lamented how difficult it was for ruler and minister to find one another. Was this not to take inquiry and study as essential? Thus, honoring one’s moral nature indeed provides the foundation for inquiry and study, while inquiry and study are truly essential to honoring one’s moral nature. The two serve one another in turn; neither can properly be neglected in favor of the other. Measured against the transmitted teaching of refined discernment, single-mindedness, and holding fast to the Mean, they accord across a thousand years. The successive sage emperors inherited this teaching and made it an enduring rule of the imperial house. Could the boundless blessings they thereby bequeathed to ten thousand generations have arisen merely by chance?

Ah! The learning of emperors and kings differs from that of ordinary scholars in humble dress. If they merely busy themselves with the peripheral matters of memorization, recitation, and literary composition, this will not enable them to investigate principle fully and establish the foundation of all under Heaven. Yet what brings this learning to fulfillment, from beginning to end, lies also in reverent attentiveness. One must reflect that the Lord on High watches over you: then the heart will be filled with awe and will not dare grow negligent. One must regard the common people as though they were wounded: then the heart will be filled with anxious concern and will not dare act without restraint. These are all great principles transmitted from one emperor or king to another, essential ways by which the imperial ancestors bequeathed well-being to their descendants; they must not be neglected.

Now the Son of Heaven reigns above, perceptive and wise, revering Heaven and caring for the people, ably carrying forward the glorious achievements of his predecessors, and…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
□□□儒臣又皆素抱格心之學其
經筵所講者諒必有及於此久矣此固天下
臣民所同望而草茅之懷尤有未釋焉者
也倘得旅進于
廷則尚有大於此者當為次第陳之
第二問
吳孔祥
同考試官訓導鄭批偽書雜出觀者味其詞義
考其世之先後自不能逃諸子中理之言當不以人
===
廢胷中無真見其不眩於疑似取舍者幾希此篇辨
悉殆邃於理學者乎宜錄以傳
同考試官教諭林批子書一策昧者不知所答
為大言者又輕之以為不足答而於諸子之真偽得
失竟無折衷子能辨析而末歸重於六經之說其亦
爰諸手而的有卓見者歟噫必子之言出而後諸子
不足以惑人矣
考試官教諭魏批三墳以下的辨真偽不取
荀子之言更出問目之外古所謂茂異者非若士耶
punctuated:
□□□儒臣又皆素抱格心之學，其經筵所講者，諒必有及於此久矣。此固天下臣民所同望，而草茅之懷尤有未釋焉者也。倘得旅進于廷，則尚有大於此者，當為次第陳之。
第二問
吳孔祥
同考試官訓導鄭批：偽書雜出，觀者味其詞義，考其世之先後，自不能逃。諸子中理之言，當不以人廢。胷中無真見，其不眩於疑似取舍者幾希。此篇辨悉，殆邃於理學者乎？宜錄以傳。
同考試官教諭林批：子書一策，昧者不知所答，為大言者又輕之，以為不足答，而於諸子之真偽得失竟無折衷。子能辨析，而末歸重於六經之說，其亦爰諸手而的有卓見者歟？噫！必子之言出，而後諸子不足以惑人矣。
考試官教諭魏批：三墳以下，的辨真偽；不取荀子之言，更出問目之外。古所謂茂異者，非若士耶？
translation_en:
…[three illegible characters] the Confucian officials, too, have long cultivated the learning by which the ruler’s heart is rectified. Surely their lectures at the Classics Colloquium must have addressed this long ago. This is indeed the shared hope of all officials and subjects throughout the realm, yet I, a humble man outside office, still have concerns that remain unresolved. Should I be permitted to advance into court among the others, I shall have still greater matters to set forth in due order.
Second policy question
Wu Kongxiang
Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Assistant Instructor: Spurious books have appeared among the genuine. If readers ponder their language and meaning and examine the chronological sequence of their periods, the forgeries cannot escape detection. Statements by the various philosophical masters that accord with principle should not be rejected on account of the men who made them. Without true insight within, few can avoid being bewildered by doubtful resemblances when deciding what to accept or reject. This essay makes its distinctions thoroughly. Might its author be deeply versed in the Learning of Principle? It should be recorded and circulated.
Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: Faced with this policy question on the writings of the philosophical masters, the ignorant do not know how to answer, while those given to grand pronouncements dismiss it as unworthy of an answer. Thus they ultimately reach no sound judgment on the authenticity and merits or faults of these writings. You can distinguish and analyze them, and finally give primacy to the teachings of the Six Classics. Might you also have grasped the matter in hand [?] and truly possess outstanding insight? Ah! Only once your words appear will the philosophical masters cease to be capable of misleading people.
Comment by Examiner Wei, Instructor: From the Three Tombs onward, you distinguish genuine writings from spurious ones with certainty. Your rejection of Xunzi’s statements goes even beyond the scope of the question. Are not those whom the ancients called outstanding and exceptional men scholars such as you? …

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
柄文之責可少逭矣
考試官教諭林批策以尊孔氏黜百家為定
論佳士佳士
著書有無據者論其是非君子所弗信也
立言有近理者論其可否君子所弗棄也
自夫聖人作經之後書有真僞之殊然一
以其道而論之雖號稱名儒未必不爲之
誣而况其他乎槩以其人而論之雖其言
合於儒者亦未必不在棄絶之中矣是豈
===
可不深辨之哉請以是而復明問所及今
夫以山墳為伏羲以氣墳為神農以形墳
為黄帝之書其辭不類淺陋無稽孔子繫
易但云伏羲氏畫八卦神農為耒耜黄帝
垂衣裳未嘗論有所謂三墳書也孔子不
言安國何據而言之耶夏小正書孔子有
取於夏時者以建寅之月為歳首非誠謂
此書也果夏之遺書何不編於禹貢胤征
之間倘見此書何不曰得小正而曰吾得
punctuated:
柄文之責可少逭矣。

考試官教諭林批：策以尊孔氏、黜百家為定論。佳士！佳士！

著書有無據者，論其是非，君子所弗信也；立言有近理者，論其可否，君子所弗棄也。自夫聖人作經之後，書有真僞之殊。然一以其道而論之，雖號稱名儒，未必不爲之誣，而况其他乎？槩以其人而論之，雖其言合於儒者，亦未必不在棄絶之中矣。是豈可不深辨之哉？請以是而復明問所及。今夫以山墳為伏羲，以氣墳為神農，以形墳為黄帝之書，其辭不類，淺陋無稽。孔子繫易，但云伏羲氏畫八卦，神農為耒耜，黄帝垂衣裳，未嘗論有所謂三墳書也。孔子不言，安國何據而言之耶？夏小正書，孔子有取於夏時者，以建寅之月為歳首，非誠謂此書也。果夏之遺書，何不編於禹貢、胤征之間？倘見此書，何不曰「得小正」，而曰「吾得
translation_en:
…I may now be somewhat absolved of my responsibility for judging literary compositions.

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: This policy essay takes honoring Confucius and rejecting the Hundred Schools as its settled conclusion. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!

When writings lack a basis, the gentleman, in judging their truth or falsehood, does not trust them. When statements approach sound principle, the gentleman, in judging their acceptability, does not discard them. Ever since the sages composed the Classics, books have differed in authenticity. Yet if we judge them solely by the Way they express, even works attributed to renowned Confucian scholars may prove to be false attributions—how much more so other works! If we judge them indiscriminately by their authors, even statements consonant with Confucian teaching may find themselves rejected. How could we fail to distinguish these matters carefully? Allow me to use this approach to respond to the matters raised in your illuminating question.

Now, the Mountain Record (Shan fen) is attributed to Fuxi, the Vital Energy Record (Qi fen) to Shennong, and the Form Record (Xing fen) to Huangdi. Their language is incongruous, shallow, and without foundation. In his Appended Statements to the Changes, Confucius merely says that Fuxi drew the eight trigrams, Shennong made plowing implements, and Huangdi let his upper and lower garments hang down. He never discusses the existence of books called the Three Records (San fen). If Confucius did not mention them, on what grounds did Kong Anguo speak of them?

As for the Lesser Calendar of Xia (Xia xiaozheng), what Confucius approved in the Xia calendar was its use of the month designated by the earthly branch yin as the first month of the year; he was not actually referring to this book. If it really were a surviving book of the Xia dynasty, why was it not included between the Tribute of Yu and the Punitive Expedition of Yin? If he had seen this book, why did he not say, ‘I obtained the Lesser Calendar,’ but instead say, ‘I obtained…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
夏時焉鄭康成抑何解而信之耶汲冢十
卷論載周事如世俘篇曰馘魔俘人皆以
萬計豈謂武王而有是殘酷乎官人篇曰
醉酒以觀其恭縱色以觀其常豈謂周公
而以此取人乎劉向不當以為刪定之餘
也三略三篇雜援軍讖其曰奸雄相稱曰
霸者制士以權曰非譎奇無以破姦非陰
謀無以成功夫讖書起於戰國之後太公
之時曾有此乎中略之末謂三略為衰世
===
===
而作太公之佐文王果衰世乎三山施子
美何至註釋以炫其博也程本與孔子同
時乃所傾蓋而敬之者其言宜有過人者十
篇之中如語道德則頗襲老列之旨專對
則倣左氏之文辨黃帝鑄鼎之事不能直
排其謬傅會不經而乃以為子華子之書
信乎晁公武謂元豊以後人所誣也曾子
在孔門獨得其正傳其言必皆純粹者十
篇之中言孝尤備如曰喜之而觀其不誣
punctuated: 夏時焉」？鄭康成抑何解而信之耶？汲冢十卷，論載周事。如《世俘篇》曰：「馘魔俘人，皆以萬計。」豈謂武王而有是殘酷乎？《官人篇》曰：「醉酒以觀其恭，縱色以觀其常。」豈謂周公而以此取人乎？劉向不當以為刪定之餘也。《三略》三篇，雜援軍讖。其曰：「奸雄相稱。」曰：「霸者制士以權。」曰：「非譎奇無以破姦，非陰謀無以成功。」夫讖書起於戰國之後，太公之時曾有此乎？《中略》之末謂《三略》為衰世而作，太公之佐文王，果衰世乎？三山施子美何至註釋以炫其博也？程本與孔子同時，乃所傾蓋而敬之者，其言宜有過人者。十篇之中，如語道德，則頗襲老列之旨；專對，則倣左氏之文。辨黃帝鑄鼎之事，不能直排其謬，傅會不經，而乃以為子華子之書。信乎晁公武謂元豊以後人所誣也！曾子在孔門獨得其正傳，其言必皆純粹者。十篇之中，言孝尤備。如曰：「喜之而觀其不誣
translation_en:
…“the calendar of Xia therein”? What understanding did Zheng Kangcheng have that led him to believe it?

The ten juan from the Ji tomb discuss and record the affairs of Zhou. For example, the chapter “Captives of the Conquest” says: “Severed ears [?] and human captives were all counted in tens of thousands.” Could King Wu have been so cruel? The chapter “Assessing Men for Office” says: “Make him drunk to observe his respectfulness; give him free rein with women to observe his constancy.” Could the Duke of Zhou have selected men by such means? Liu Xiang ought not to have regarded this as material left over from the editorial selection.

The three chapters of the Three Strategies (Sanlüe) indiscriminately cite military prophetic writings. They say: “The treacherous and the mighty are matched with one another [?]”; “A hegemon controls his officers through expediency”; and “Without deception and extraordinary devices there is no way to defeat treachery; without secret plots there is no way to achieve success.” Now, prophetic writings arose after the Warring States period. Could such things already have existed in the time of Taigong? The end of the “Middle Strategy” says that the Three Strategies was written for an age of decline. Was the time when Taigong assisted King Wen really an age of decline? Why did Shi Zimei of Sanshan go so far as to annotate it to display his erudition?

Cheng Ben lived at the same time as Confucius and was someone whom Confucius respected when they met with their carriage canopies inclined toward one another. His words ought therefore to have surpassed those of others. Yet among the ten chapters, discussions of the Way and virtue largely borrow the purport of Laozi and Liezi, while passages on diplomatic responses imitate the writing of Master Zuo. In examining the story of the Yellow Emperor casting a tripod, the text fails to reject its absurdity outright and instead offers strained, unfounded explanations. Yet it is taken to be the book of Zihuazi! How true is Chao Gongwu’s statement that it was falsely attributed by someone after the Yuanfeng era!

Among Confucius’s disciples, Zengzi alone received the orthodox transmission; his words must therefore all have been pure and unadulterated. Among the ten chapters, the discussion of filial piety is especially full. For example, it says: “Make him happy and observe whether he refrains from falsehood…”

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
怒之而觀其不惛近諸色而觀其不踰飲食
之而觀其有常决非曾子之言而或者成
於漢儒之手也據名責實而直以大道論
之諸書真僞自無所匿而何惑人心之有
哉至若荀卿之著荀子剽掠聖經肆然居
於孔子之道沛乎若有所宗淵乎執之無
窮要其大旨則謂人之性惡以仁義爲僞
其言似是而實非世欲擯悖道之書而不
用必自荀卿始而何言之足取乎孫子十
===
三篇所論先計謀而後攻戰先智謀而後
料敵用兵料敵周備明白雖不足與於仁
義之師苟以之戰則非良將乎吳起受學
於曾子其書雖間談仁義而豈知仁義以
自律及觀在德不在險之論信乎戰國時
之名言也慎到亦韓非之流墮於曲學而
豈知仁義之爲治其謂立天子以爲天下
是由儒者君爲輕之意也尹文子一卷謂
任道不足以治而用法術權勢劉向斷爲
punctuated: 怒之而觀其不惛，近諸色而觀其不踰，飲食之而觀其有常」，决非曾子之言，而或者成於漢儒之手也。據名責實，而直以大道論之，諸書真僞自無所匿，而何惑人心之有哉？至若荀卿之著《荀子》，剽掠聖經，肆然居於孔子之道，沛乎若有所宗，淵乎執之無窮。要其大旨，則謂人之性惡，以仁義爲僞。其言似是而實非。世欲擯悖道之書而不用，必自荀卿始，而何言之足取乎？《孫子》十三篇，所論先計謀而後攻戰，先智謀而後料敵，用兵料敵，周備明白。雖不足與於仁義之師，苟以之戰，則非良將乎？吳起受學於曾子，其書雖間談仁義，而豈知仁義以自律？及觀「在德不在險」之論，信乎戰國時之名言也。慎到亦韓非之流，墮於曲學，而豈知仁義之爲治？其謂立天子以爲天下，是由儒者君爲輕之意也。《尹文子》一卷，謂任道不足以治，而用法術權勢，劉向斷爲
translation_en:
…“Provoke him to anger and observe whether he remains clear-headed; bring him near alluring beauty and observe whether he transgresses; give him food and drink and observe whether he maintains his constancy.” These are certainly not the words of Zengzi; perhaps they were composed by Han Confucian scholars. If we examine the substance against the name and judge directly by the Great Way, the authenticity or falsity of these books will have nowhere to hide. How, then, could they confuse people’s minds?

As for Xun Qing’s composition of the Xunzi, he plundered the sages’ classics and brazenly claimed a place within the Way of Confucius. His writing flows abundantly, as though grounded in some authoritative source, and seems profound, as though its implications were inexhaustible. Yet its central purport is that human nature is evil and that benevolence and righteousness are artificial constructs. His words appear correct but are actually wrong. If the world wishes to reject books that contravene the Way and cease using them, it must begin with Xun Qing. What words of his, then, are worth adopting?

The thirteen chapters of the Sunzi place planning before attack and battle, and intelligent strategy before assessing the enemy. Their treatment of deploying troops and assessing the enemy is comprehensive and clear. Although this falls short of what is required for an army guided by benevolence and righteousness, would someone who fought according to it not be a good general?

Wu Qi studied under Zengzi. Although his book occasionally discusses benevolence and righteousness, how could he have understood using them to regulate his own conduct? Yet when we examine his argument that security “lies in virtue, not in defensible terrain,” it is indeed a memorable saying of the Warring States period.

Shen Dao, too, belonged to the same school as Han Fei and fell into distorted learning. How could he have understood governing through benevolence and righteousness? His statement that the Son of Heaven is established for the sake of all under Heaven, however, follows the Confucian idea that the ruler is of lesser importance.

The Yin Wenzi, in one fascicle, holds that reliance on the Way is insufficient for governing and instead employs laws, techniques, power, and positional authority. Liu Xiang classified it as …

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
刑名家者也但其爲民之心頗切末章□
中時君之弊使舉而行之亦足以善其國
而仲長統獨好之則過矣鄧析子所著二
篇以干諸侯實爲嚴酷之行如曰令煩則
民詐政擾則民不定又曰目貴明耳貴聰
心貴公雖其言足以資治而要其人則李
斯之輩矣呂不韋乗勢致富貴而行不謹
功業無可道而著於春秋亦有足取者觀
其節喪哀死篇譏厚葬之弊其勿躬篇言
===
人君之要在于任人用民篇言刑罰不如
德禮達鬱分職篇皆盡君人之道吳子以
下凡言之幾於理者君子不當因其人而
棄之而荀卿則固在黜列也學者格物之
要舍是而不辨辨而不慎則作者借名以
惑人而僞書滋蔓矣于其人而不于其言
則天下皆棄人矣雖然書之僞者不必信
焉而諸子之書有志者顧以是爲景慕也
哉六經之言本於道德所以正人心而淑
punctuated: 刑名家者也。但其爲民之心頗切，末章□中時君之弊，使舉而行之，亦足以善其國，而仲長統獨好之，則過矣。鄧析子所著二篇，以干諸侯，實爲嚴酷之行。如曰：「令煩則民詐，政擾則民不定。」又曰：「目貴明，耳貴聰，心貴公。」雖其言足以資治，而要其人，則李斯之輩矣。呂不韋乗勢致富貴，而行不謹，功業無可道，而著於《春秋》，亦有足取者。觀其《節喪》《哀死》篇，譏厚葬之弊；其《勿躬》篇，言人君之要在于任人；《用民》篇，言刑罰不如德禮；《達鬱》《分職》篇，皆盡君人之道。吳子以下，凡言之幾於理者，君子不當因其人而棄之，而荀卿則固在黜列也。學者格物之要，舍是而不辨，辨而不慎，則作者借名以惑人，而僞書滋蔓矣。于其人而不于其言，則天下皆棄人矣。雖然，書之僞者不必信焉，而諸子之書，有志者顧以是爲景慕也哉？六經之言，本於道德，所以正人心而淑
translation_en: …a member of the School of Forms and Names. Yet his concern for the people is quite earnest. The final chapter □ exposes the faults of the rulers of his day [?]; if its proposals were put into practice, they would suffice to improve a state. Zhongchang Tong’s exclusive fondness for it, however, went too far. The two chapters written by Deng Xizi to seek favor with the feudal lords in fact advocate harsh and cruel practices. He says, for example: “When ordinances are burdensome, the people become deceitful; when government is intrusive, the people cannot be settled.” He also says: “What matters in the eyes is clear sight; in the ears, keen hearing; in the mind, impartiality.” Although his words can aid government, the man himself was, in essence, of the same sort as Li Si. Lü Buwei took advantage of circumstances to attain wealth and eminence, but was careless in his conduct. His achievements offer nothing worth recounting, yet what he set down in the Spring and Autumn Annals contains things worth adopting. His chapters “Moderation in Funerals” and “Mourning the Dead” criticize the abuses of lavish burial. “Do Not Act Personally” explains that the ruler’s essential task lies in entrusting responsibilities to others; “Employing the People” explains that punishments are inferior to virtue and ritual propriety. “Clearing Obstructions” and “Dividing Responsibilities” both fully expound the way of ruling others. From Wuzi onward, whenever their words approach sound principle, the gentleman ought not to reject them on account of the men who spoke them. Xun Qing, however, certainly belongs among those to be excluded. The essential task for scholars in investigating things is to make these distinctions. If they neglect this and fail to distinguish, or distinguish without care, authors will borrow names to mislead people, and spurious books will proliferate. If one judges by the person rather than by his words [?], everyone under Heaven will be a person to discard. Nevertheless, spurious books need not be believed; but should those with high aspirations really take the writings of the various masters as objects of admiration? The words of the Six Classics are rooted in the Way and virtue, serving to rectify people’s minds and improve…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
皆當世執事所謂聖人著書其大道炳如日
星是其師法者乎區區管見不足以語格
物之學唯進而教之幸甚
第三問
張佾
同考試官教諭吳批士風一策正欲觀諸士子
所養子能於古之廉退者悉數無遺而獨推重於靖
節元城尤為有見噫子其尚友而知所向方者乎
同考試官教諭陳批廉退之行士君子不可一日
===
離者士子多據題敷荅此獨以有所為無所為立說末
尤歸重於無所為而為之士亦可以占其平日之所養矣
同考試官學正周批節行廉退古人以為第一事
而今或忽焉此發策之所願聞而求其故者子獨言之
痛切又推其本之有自其真不易之論哉
考試官教諭魏批援古道今而發於奮迅激
昂之氣盖必能砥柱於中流者主司當拭目俟之
考試官教諭林批歷叙卓異之行以風人心
有志之士也
punctuated:
皆當世。執事所謂聖人著書，其大道炳如日星，是其師法者乎？區區管見，不足以語格物之學，唯進而教之，幸甚。

第三問
張佾

同考試官教諭吳批：士風一策，正欲觀諸士子所養。子能於古之廉退者悉數無遺，而獨推重於靖節、元城，尤為有見。噫！子其尚友而知所向方者乎？

同考試官教諭陳批：廉退之行，士君子不可一日離者。士子多據題敷荅，此獨以有所為、無所為立說，末尤歸重於無所為而為之士，亦可以占其平日之所養矣。

同考試官學正周批：節行廉退，古人以為第一事，而今或忽焉。此發策之所願聞而求其故者。子獨言之痛切，又推其本之有自，其真不易之論哉！

考試官教諭魏批：援古道今，而發於奮迅激昂之氣，盖必能砥柱於中流者，主司當拭目俟之。

考試官教諭林批：歷叙卓異之行，以風人心，有志之士也。
translation_en:
…all in the present age [?]. The sages whose writings, as you, sir, have said, make the great Way shine as brightly as the sun and stars—are these not those whom one should take as teachers and models? My paltry, narrow views are insufficient for discussing the learning of the investigation of things. I would be most fortunate if you would offer further instruction.

Third Policy Question
Zhang Yi

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: This policy question on the ethos of scholars was intended precisely to reveal what the candidates have cultivated within themselves. You enumerate exhaustively the men of antiquity known for integrity and modest withdrawal, yet give particular weight to Jingjie and Yuancheng. This shows exceptional discernment. Ah! Are you one who befriends the worthy of antiquity and knows the direction he should follow?

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: Integrity and modest withdrawal are qualities that a gentleman must not abandon for even a single day. Most candidates simply elaborate an answer based on the question. This candidate alone builds his argument around acting with an ulterior purpose and acting without one. At the end, he gives particular weight to scholars who act without an ulterior purpose. From this one can also judge what he has cultivated in his daily life.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: Principled conduct, integrity, and modest withdrawal were regarded by the ancients as matters of first importance, yet people today sometimes neglect them. This is what the policy question sought to hear about and whose causes it sought to investigate. You alone discuss it with piercing force, and further trace it to its underlying source. Truly, this is an argument that cannot be overturned!

Comment by Examiner Wei, Instructor: He draws upon antiquity to discuss the present, expressing himself with vigorous and impassioned spirit. Surely he will be able to stand like a pillar of rock in midstream. We examiners should watch keenly for what he will accomplish.

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: He recounts outstanding deeds in succession to influence people’s hearts. He is a scholar of aspiration.

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
欲匡世教當有以審其機欲正人心當有
以端其本蓋不審其機則無以挽天下之
變不端其本則無以定天下之經是故廉
介也恬退也乃世道轉移之機治化之汙
隆風俗之美惡繫焉管子曰四維不張國
乃滅亡則亦非細故也奚可不求所以正
人心而端其本源之地乎執事發策下詢
有及於此蓋爲世道憂敢不因明問以對
古今天下未嘗無廉介之士也亦未嘗無
===
恬退之人也然有有所爲而爲之者亦有
無所爲而爲之者據其跡而言非不曰某
廉介也某恬退也然不出於心術之正則
始雖善而不能掩其終人將指議之不暇
尚何望其變天下之俗以成治化哉惟其
無所爲而爲則其見於事者本諸心所謂
富貴不能淫貧賤不能移而世道之賴必
斯人矣嘗稽諸古孔奮守姑臧而妻子蔬
食或議之曰脂膏不潤也袁聿脩爲太常
punctuated:
欲匡世教，當有以審其機；欲正人心，當有以端其本。蓋不審其機，則無以挽天下之變；不端其本，則無以定天下之經。是故廉介也，恬退也，乃世道轉移之機，治化之汙隆、風俗之美惡繫焉。管子曰：「四維不張，國乃滅亡。」則亦非細故也，奚可不求所以正人心而端其本源之地乎？執事發策下詢，有及於此，蓋爲世道憂，敢不因明問以對？

古今天下未嘗無廉介之士也，亦未嘗無恬退之人也。然有有所爲而爲之者，亦有無所爲而爲之者。據其跡而言，非不曰某廉介也，某恬退也。然不出於心術之正，則始雖善而不能掩其終，人將指議之不暇，尚何望其變天下之俗以成治化哉？惟其無所爲而爲，則其見於事者本諸心，所謂「富貴不能淫，貧賤不能移」，而世道之賴必斯人矣。嘗稽諸古，孔奮守姑臧，而妻子蔬食，或議之曰：「脂膏不潤也。」袁聿脩爲太常
translation_en:
To rectify the moral teachings of the age, one must discern the pivotal points on which they turn; to set people’s hearts right, one must correct their root. Without discerning those pivotal points, one cannot reverse adverse changes in the world; without correcting the root, one cannot establish its enduring norms. Thus integrity and principled conduct, together with quiet restraint and withdrawal from advancement, are pivotal to changes in the moral condition of the age. The decline or flourishing of government and moral transformation, and the goodness or badness of customs, depend upon them. The Guanzi says: “If the four binding principles are not upheld, the state will perish.” This is therefore no trifling matter. How could one fail to seek the means of setting people’s hearts right and correcting their very source? In issuing your policy question and deigning to consult us, you have touched upon this matter, surely out of concern for the moral condition of the age. How could I fail to answer your discerning inquiry?

From antiquity to the present, the world has never lacked men of integrity and principle, nor people content to withdraw from advancement. Yet some act with an ulterior purpose, while others act without one. Judging by their outward conduct, one might indeed say that a certain man possesses integrity and principle, or that another is quietly unambitious. But if this conduct does not proceed from upright intentions, then, however good its beginning, it cannot conceal its eventual outcome. People will scarcely have time enough to point out and criticize their faults. How could one still expect such men to transform the world’s customs and bring about good government and moral transformation? Only when a man acts without an ulterior purpose does what appears in his deeds originate in his heart. Such is the meaning of “wealth and honor cannot corrupt him; poverty and low status cannot sway him.” These must be the men upon whom the moral condition of the age depends. I have examined examples from antiquity. When Kong Fen administered Guzang, his wife and children ate only vegetables, and someone remarked of him: “The rich grease does not moisten him”—the wealth around him brought him no enrichment. Yuan Yuxiu served as Chamberlain for Ceremonials…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
卿而辭還白紬人稱之曰今日清卿也吳
隱之為尚書而以竹為屏風皇甫無逸為
長史而斷帶為燈炷至若裴俠趙軌或號
獨立使君或稱公清如水而其人猶可想
也朱雲見時宰出峻厲之辭陶潜令彭澤
發高抗之語韓維為主簿安於恬退蘇頌
為校理惟求外補至若劉安世韋澳或無
書抵政府或不為呈身御史而其名猶未
泯也之數人者清風高節雖心術未盡察
===
===
其微而狂瀾砥柱世道亦藉之而少補此
固機之一轉移耳然就其中不容以疵議
者吾得二人焉其陶淵明乎劉安世乎是
又不可以一節盡之洪惟我
國家以道德成人才以廉退勵士行為士者
爭相濯磨以建勳立名視古所稱殆遠過
之何邇年人心一變浮風漸漓苞苴媚竈
遂忘其恥者且將日增而月盛矣然履霜
之戒君子慎之此執事所以為今日之慮
punctuated: 卿，而辭還白紬，人稱之曰：「今日清卿也。」吳隱之為尚書，而以竹為屏風；皇甫無逸為長史，而斷帶為燈炷。至若裴俠、趙軌，或號獨立使君，或稱公清如水，而其人猶可想也。朱雲見時宰，出峻厲之辭；陶潜令彭澤，發高抗之語；韓維為主簿，安於恬退；蘇頌為校理，惟求外補。至若劉安世、韋澳，或無書抵政府，或不為呈身御史，而其名猶未泯也。之數人者，清風高節，雖心術未盡察其微，而狂瀾砥柱，世道亦藉之而少補。此固機之一轉移耳。然就其中不容以疵議者，吾得二人焉：其陶淵明乎？劉安世乎？是又不可以一節盡之。洪惟我國家，以道德成人才，以廉退勵士行。為士者爭相濯磨，以建勳立名，視古所稱，殆遠過之。何邇年人心一變，浮風漸漓，苞苴媚竈，遂忘其恥者，且將日增而月盛矣？然履霜之戒，君子慎之。此執事所以為今日之慮
translation_en:
…Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, yet declined and returned the white silk; people praised him, saying, “He is the incorruptible minister of our day.” Wu Yinzhi served as a minister but used bamboo for his screen; Huangfu Wuyi served as an administrator but cut up his belt to make lamp wicks. As for Pei Xia and Zhao Gui, one was styled “the peerless prefect,” and the other was praised as “a lord as pure as water.” We can still picture what manner of men they were. Zhu Yun, when meeting the chief minister of his day, spoke stern and uncompromising words; Tao Qian, when magistrate of Pengze, uttered proud and defiant words. Han Wei, as a registrar, was content with quiet withdrawal; Su Song, as a collator, sought only appointment outside the capital. As for Liu Anshi and Wei Ao, one sent no letters to the chief ministers, while the other refused to become a “self-presenting censor”—one who sought advancement by presenting himself to the powerful. Their names have still not faded.

These men displayed an untainted character and lofty integrity. Although we cannot fully discern the subtleties of their inward motives, they stood like a rock amid raging currents, and the moral order of the world gained some support from them. This was assuredly a turning of the pivotal impulse. Yet among them I find two who admit of no reproach: are they not Tao Yuanming and Liu Anshi? Their worth, moreover, cannot be encompassed by a single instance of integrity.

I reverently reflect that our dynasty develops men of talent through moral virtue and encourages scholars’ conduct through incorruptibility and modest withdrawal. Scholars vie with one another in cleansing and refining themselves, seeking to establish meritorious achievements and lasting reputations; compared with those praised in antiquity, they have perhaps far surpassed them. Why, then, have people’s hearts changed in recent years, with frivolous habits growing ever more debased, so that those who offer bribes and flatter the powerful—“paying court to the kitchen god”—forget their shame and are about to multiply day by day and month by month? Yet the gentleman heeds the warning conveyed by treading on frost, knowing that hard ice will follow. This is why you, honored examiners, are concerned about the present day…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
也此正愚生之所謂審其機者也而所以
端其本者豈他求哉亦繫乎在上之人爾
蓋好惡不示無以定其趨向黜陟不嚴無
以别其淑慝必也杜飾詐則考名實之歸
振超異則立保薦之法表率之地不為虛
文而觀法之士惟求實踐使廉介者盡用
而嗜利者不容恬退者咸收而希進者必
抑則鼓舞之下懦士將奮而企矣鄙夫亦
從而變矣由是在野在位無非正人又何
===
患治化不日隆風俗不日厚乎雖然此特
以待有所為而為之士也若夫無所為而
為者雖無文王猶興又在乎
聖君賢相搜羅之以為世道計爾謹對
第四問
梅賢
同考試官訓導李批賈陸之論已定於蘇氏此策
又能發其未盡之意且善用題中常變二字寫出二子
忠愛之心蓋不可以尋常應舉之文求之也
punctuated:
也。此正愚生之所謂審其機者也。而所以端其本者，豈他求哉？亦繫乎在上之人爾。蓋好惡不示，無以定其趨向；黜陟不嚴，無以别其淑慝。必也杜飾詐，則考名實之歸；振超異，則立保薦之法。表率之地不為虛文，而觀法之士惟求實踐。使廉介者盡用，而嗜利者不容；恬退者咸收，而希進者必抑。則鼓舞之下，懦士將奮而企矣，鄙夫亦從而變矣。由是在野在位無非正人，又何患治化不日隆、風俗不日厚乎？雖然，此特以待有所為而為之士也。若夫無所為而為者，雖無文王猶興，又在乎聖君賢相搜羅之，以為世道計爾。謹對。

第四問
梅賢

同考試官訓導李批：賈陸之論已定於蘇氏，此策又能發其未盡之意，且善用題中常變二字，寫出二子忠愛之心，蓋不可以尋常應舉之文求之也。
translation_en:
…This is precisely what I, your humble student, mean by scrutinizing the critical turning point. As for setting the root right, why seek elsewhere? This too depends upon those above. Unless they make their likes and dislikes clear, there is no way to give direction to men’s aspirations; unless dismissal and promotion are rigorously administered, there is no way to distinguish the good from the wicked. To put an end to deceptive appearances, one must examine whether reputation accords with reality; to advance exceptional men, one must establish procedures for guaranteeing and recommending candidates. Those in positions that serve as models must not engage in empty formalities, while scholars who look to them as examples must seek only to put principles into practice. Let all men of integrity and firm principle be employed, and allow no place for those who crave profit; let all who are content to remain withdrawn be recruited, and invariably restrain those who seek advancement. Under such encouragement, even timid scholars will rouse themselves and aspire to virtue, and base men will likewise change. Thus, whether out of office or in office, all will be upright men. Why then worry that good government and moral transformation will not flourish daily, or that customs will not daily grow more wholesome? Nevertheless, these measures are intended only for scholars who act with some ulterior purpose. As for those who act without an ulterior purpose, they rise to virtue even without a King Wen. It remains for the sage ruler and worthy ministers to seek them out and gather them in, taking thought for the moral order of the age. Respectfully submitted in reply.

Fourth Question
Mei Xian

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Assistant Instructor: Master Su has already settled the assessment of Jia and Lu. Yet this policy essay brings out meanings he did not fully explore. Moreover, it makes skillful use of the two terms in the question, “constancy” and “change,” to portray the two men’s loyal and devoted hearts. It certainly cannot be judged by the standards of an ordinary examination composition.

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭魏批即今以按古用古以法今
策士意也豈在編簡文字間邪子知之而議論引斷
有補於今賈陸二子當不悼其不遇於當時矣經世
者采而用之必子之言夫
考試官教諭林批論斷賈陸才辯學術與遭
際之詳皆卓有的見若二子聞之亦將有以服其心矣
人才出乎一代而論有定於後人論議厄
於一時而用有資於後世甚矣豪傑之才
不易得也吾於漢而得賈誼於唐而得陸
贄焉二子者學足以引翼時君而知之者
則未真才足以康乂一世而用之者則未
盡故其終身之定論不見於當時而平生
之論議猶足爲百世有天下者之資也執
事發策以二子爲問而必稱其致用之學
得非有忠君愛國之心欲起斯人而與之
論當世之務乎朱子以尚論古人爲格物
之一端風簷寸晷使得盡其愚則不但爲
致知之助而已也竊嘗尋繹蘇氏父子稱
punctuated:
考試官教諭魏批：即今以按古，用古以法今，策士意也，豈在編簡文字間邪？子知之，而議論引斷，有補於今。賈陸二子，當不悼其不遇於當時矣。經世者采而用之，必子之言夫！

考試官教諭林批：論斷賈陸才辯、學術與遭際之詳，皆卓有的見。若二子聞之，亦將有以服其心矣。

人才出乎一代，而論有定於後人；論議厄於一時，而用有資於後世。甚矣，豪傑之才不易得也！吾於漢而得賈誼，於唐而得陸贄焉。二子者，學足以引翼時君，而知之者則未真；才足以康乂一世，而用之者則未盡。故其終身之定論不見於當時，而平生之論議猶足爲百世有天下者之資也。執事發策，以二子爲問，而必稱其致用之學，得非有忠君愛國之心，欲起斯人而與之論當世之務乎？朱子以尚論古人爲格物之一端，風簷寸晷，使得盡其愚，則不但爲致知之助而已也。竊嘗尋繹蘇氏父子稱
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Wei, Instructor: To examine antiquity in light of the present, and to use antiquity as a guide for the present: this is the purpose of testing scholars with policy questions. How could it lie merely among written texts? You understand this, and your arguments and conclusions contribute something useful to the present. Jia Yi and Lu Zhi should therefore have no cause to lament their failure to find recognition in their own times. Surely those who order the world will adopt and put your words to use!

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: Your assessments of Jia Yi’s and Lu Zhi’s talents and eloquence, their learning, and the particulars of their fortunes all show outstanding and precise insight. If the two men heard them, they too would be inwardly convinced.

Talented men emerge in one age, but their definitive appraisal rests with later generations; their arguments encounter obstruction at one time, but their application benefits later ages. How very difficult it is to find men of exceptional talent! In the Han I find Jia Yi, and in the Tang, Lu Zhi. These two men possessed learning sufficient to guide and assist the rulers of their time, yet those who recognized them did not truly understand them; their talents were sufficient to bring peace and order to an age, yet those who employed them did not use them fully. Thus no definitive judgment of their lives emerged in their own day, while the arguments they advanced throughout their lives remain resources for rulers of the realm for a hundred generations.

You, sir, have issued a policy question concerning these two men, expressly praising their learning directed toward practical application. Is this not because, with hearts loyal to the ruler and devoted to the country, you wish to bring these men back to life and discuss the affairs of the present age with them? Master Zhu regarded considering and appraising the ancients as one aspect of investigating things. If, beneath these wind-swept eaves and in the brief time allotted, I may fully express my humble thoughts, this will do more than merely help extend my knowledge. I have ventured to ponder the words in which the father and son of the Su family praised …

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
二子之言而推其意曰經與權聖人之道
也董子以經晁錯以權誼獨兼之而且無
流為迂詐之失洵之稱誼者果當耶智與
辯致用之才也子房以智賈誼以辯贄則
兼之而且有文而不疎之美軾之推贄者
果是耶又嘗求其告君之言而得其救時
之意蓋天下之常變猶天道之陰晴也和
風麗日有時而變處常而狃於常可乎迅
雷驚霆或不崇朝處變而安於變可乎當
===
文帝之時海內富庶黎民醇厚固常情安
享太平之時也而誼也長慮却顧其論國
勢也諸王國大勢將難制則曰可為痛哭
匈奴為患威令不遠則曰可為流涕其論
時務也禁僭侈定經制教太子崇德教論
堂陛遠近之等辨公卿刑譴之過則曰可
為長太息也忠誠激發若有不測之憂言
論慷慨以為必至之患蓋不狃於常而以
變處夫常者矣當德宗之時戎馬交馳財
punctuated: 二子之言而推其意曰：經與權，聖人之道也。董子以經，晁錯以權，誼獨兼之，而且無流為迂詐之失。洵之稱誼者果當耶？智與辯，致用之才也。子房以智，賈誼以辯，贄則兼之，而且有文而不疎之美。軾之推贄者果是耶？又嘗求其告君之言，而得其救時之意。蓋天下之常變，猶天道之陰晴也。和風麗日，有時而變，處常而狃於常可乎？迅雷驚霆，或不崇朝，處變而安於變可乎？當文帝之時，海內富庶，黎民醇厚，固常情安享太平之時也。而誼也長慮却顧，其論國勢也，諸王國大，勢將難制，則曰可為痛哭；匈奴為患，威令不遠，則曰可為流涕。其論時務也，禁僭侈，定經制，教太子，崇德教，論堂陛遠近之等，辨公卿刑譴之過，則曰可為長太息也。忠誠激發，若有不測之憂；言論慷慨，以為必至之患。蓋不狃於常，而以變處夫常者矣。當德宗之時，戎馬交馳，財
translation_en:
…their words in praise of the two men, and sought their meaning as follows: abiding principles and discretionary judgment constitute the Way of the sages. Master Dong Zhongshu excelled in abiding principles, and Chao Cuo in discretionary judgment; Jia Yi alone combined both, without falling into the faults of impracticality or deceit. Was Su Xun’s praise of Jia Yi truly fitting? Wisdom and eloquence are talents for practical service. Zifang excelled in wisdom, and Jia Yi in eloquence; Lu Zhi combined both, and also possessed the virtue of literary accomplishment without neglect of practical detail. Was Su Shi’s esteem for Lu Zhi truly justified?

I have also examined their words of counsel to their sovereigns and discerned their intention to remedy the troubles of their times. Stability and upheaval in the realm are like cloudy and clear weather in the course of Heaven. Gentle breezes and bright sunshine sometimes change: when circumstances are stable, can one become complacent in that stability? Sudden thunder and startling thunderclaps may not last even a morning: when circumstances are unsettled, can one accept that upheaval as permanent?

In Emperor Wen’s time, all within the seas was prosperous and populous, and the common people were sincere and honest. By ordinary reckoning, this was indeed a time to enjoy peace securely. Yet Jia Yi considered the distant future and looked back to the past. In discussing the condition of the state, he declared that the kingdoms of the princes were so large that they would become difficult to control: this, he said, was cause for bitter weeping. The Xiongnu posed a threat, and imperial authority and commands did not reach far: this, he said, was cause for shedding tears. In discussing the affairs of the day, he urged prohibiting extravagance that transgressed distinctions of rank, establishing enduring institutions, educating the heir apparent, and promoting moral instruction. He discussed the gradations of proximity and distance between the sovereign and his ministers, figured as the hall and its steps, and distinguished the errors in subjecting dukes and high ministers to punishment and censure. These matters, he said, were cause for long, deep sighs. His loyal sincerity stirred him as though unforeseen troubles threatened; his words were impassioned, treating these dangers as calamities certain to arrive. He thus refused to grow complacent amid stability, and dealt with stable circumstances with upheaval in mind. In Emperor Dezong’s time, warhorses galloped to and fro, and financial resources…

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
力俱困固常情坐觀成敗之秋也而贄也
殫精竭思其論邊備也措置課責之有乖
而兵冗財匱者備陳不均遙制之有失而
將多力分者悉舉其論恤民也登稅數停
加徵減緡錢稱折估重斂移徵之政徵役
科配之條無不縷析而言也却戎保國之
謀皆出於經綸之妙惜民重本之論一發
乎忠愛之心蓋不安於變而欲以常濟其
變者矣嗚呼誼之策雖未可擬皐夔之謨
===
謨而亦可爲漢庭之藥石使其人大用焉
不但預消七國之禍亦可以庶幾三代之
風惜哉文帝竟使有梁傅之行此漢之止
於漢也贄之奏雖未可方伊傅之訓誥而
亦可爲唐室之龜鑑使其言盡行焉不但
克平寇亂之功亦可以再覩貞觀之治惜
哉德宗卒使有忠州之貶此興元之止於
興元也今之時固非德宗之時亦未可比
文帝之治雖我
punctuated: 力俱困，固常情坐觀成敗之秋也。而贄也殫精竭思，其論邊備也，措置課責之有乖而兵冗財匱者備陳，不均遙制之有失而將多力分者悉舉。其論恤民也，登稅數、停加徵、減緡錢、稱折估，重斂移徵之政、徵役科配之條，無不縷析而言也。却戎保國之謀，皆出於經綸之妙；惜民重本之論，一發乎忠愛之心。蓋不安於變，而欲以常濟其變者矣。嗚呼！誼之策雖未可擬皐夔之謨謨，而亦可爲漢庭之藥石。使其人大用焉，不但預消七國之禍，亦可以庶幾三代之風。惜哉！文帝竟使有梁傅之行，此漢之止於漢也。贄之奏雖未可方伊傅之訓誥，而亦可爲唐室之龜鑑。使其言盡行焉，不但克平寇亂之功，亦可以再覩貞觀之治。惜哉！德宗卒使有忠州之貶，此興元之止於興元也。今之時固非德宗之時，亦未可比文帝之治。雖我
translation_en:
…and strength were alike exhausted: this was indeed a time when ordinary men would sit back and watch success or failure unfold. Yet Lu Zhi exhausted his energies and applied all his thought. In discussing frontier defenses, he fully explained how faulty arrangements and demands for accountability had produced superfluous troops and depleted finances; he enumerated every instance in which unequal treatment and misguided control from afar had produced too many commanders and dispersed military strength. In discussing relief for the people, he analyzed every detail: the assessment of tax amounts [?], suspending additional levies, reducing cash payments, and fairly appraising payments commuted into goods [?], as well as policies concerning heavy exactions and transferred levies, and provisions governing labor requisitions and apportioned assessments. His plans to repel invaders and preserve the state all arose from his consummate skill in government; his arguments for cherishing the people and valuing the foundation of the state issued entirely from a loyal and loving heart. He was unwilling to rest content amid upheaval, seeking instead to use stable principles to remedy it.

Alas! Although Jia Yi’s policy proposals could not yet be ranked with the counsels of Gao Yao and Kui [the transcription repeats “counsels”], they could nonetheless serve as healing medicine for the Han court. Had he been entrusted with great responsibilities, he could not only have forestalled the disaster of the Seven Kingdoms but also have brought the realm close to the spirit of the Three Dynasties. What a pity that Emperor Wen ultimately sent him away as Grand Tutor to the Prince of Liang! This is why the Han remained merely the Han. Although Lu Zhi’s memorials could not yet be placed beside the instructions and admonitions of Yi Yin and Fu Yue, they could nonetheless serve as a guide and mirror for the Tang ruling house. Had his words all been put into practice, he could not only have achieved the suppression of banditry and rebellion but also have restored the good government of the Zhenguan era. What a pity that Dezong ultimately had him demoted to Zhongzhou! This is why the Xingyuan era remained merely Xingyuan. Our present age is certainly not the age of Dezong, nor can it be compared with Emperor Wen’s rule. Although our …

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
祖宗立國弘規非漢唐所及而法久則必弊政
久則必蠹誼猶為文帝憂今可以無憂乎
贄且為德宗圖今可以弗圖乎執事所謂
邊塵屢驚則其制匈奴措邊備之策可用
也所謂枹鼓數起則其張威令定經制之
言可用也若夫國用匱乏如其禁止僭侈
可矣民力疲困如其均節賦稅可矣軾又
嘗謂藥雖進於醫手方多傳於古人其執
事發策之意乎愚生以為今時之弊殆不
===
止此約而言之恤民之為急求賢之為大
儻欲考正於先王貽安於萬世則又當有
陳而不敢隱焉謹對
第五問
丁濬
同考試官教諭李批登明選公不拘拘於經書
章句而又兼之策者盖宏博之學經濟之才必於此
乎見之此卷前二場固佳而五策援引故實切中事
情此尤鑿鑿可行者豈可書生例目之乎意不圖
punctuated:
祖宗立國弘規，非漢唐所及，而法久則必弊，政久則必蠹。誼猶為文帝憂，今可以無憂乎？贄且為德宗圖，今可以弗圖乎？執事所謂邊塵屢驚，則其制匈奴、措邊備之策可用也；所謂枹鼓數起，則其張威令、定經制之言可用也。若夫國用匱乏，如其禁止僭侈可矣；民力疲困，如其均節賦稅可矣。軾又嘗謂：「藥雖進於醫手，方多傳於古人。」其執事發策之意乎？愚生以為今時之弊，殆不止此。約而言之，恤民之為急，求賢之為大。儻欲考正於先王，貽安於萬世，則又當有陳而不敢隱焉。謹對。

第五問
丁濬

同考試官教諭李批：登明選公，不拘拘於經書章句，而又兼之策者，盖宏博之學、經濟之才，必於此乎見之。此卷前二場固佳，而五策援引故實，切中事情，此尤鑿鑿可行者，豈可書生例目之乎？意不圖
translation_en:
…the grand principles by which our imperial ancestors founded the state surpass anything achieved by the Han and Tang. Yet laws long in force inevitably develop defects, and government long established inevitably suffers corruption. If Jia Yi still felt concern for Emperor Wen, can we now be free of concern? If Lu Zhi made plans for Emperor Dezong, can we now refrain from planning? In response to what you, sir, call repeated alarms on the frontier, their proposals for controlling the Xiongnu and arranging frontier defenses can be applied. In response to what you call the frequent sounding of war drums, their counsel on asserting authoritative commands and establishing regular institutions can be applied. As for shortages in state funds, it would suffice to follow their proposals to prohibit extravagance exceeding prescribed status; as for the exhaustion of the people's resources, it would suffice to follow their proposals to equalize and moderate taxation. Su Shi also once said: “Though medicines are administered by physicians, their prescriptions have often been handed down from the ancients.” Is this perhaps your intention in setting this policy question? I, an unworthy student, believe that the defects of our time surely extend beyond these. To put it briefly, caring for the people is the most urgent task, and seeking worthy men is the greatest. If the aim is to examine and rectify affairs according to the former kings and bequeath peace to countless generations, then I have still more to set forth and dare not conceal it. Respectfully submitted in reply.

Fifth Question
Ding Jun

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: Advancement should be discerning and selection impartial. The reason we do not confine ourselves narrowly to the chapter-and-verse interpretation of the Classics, but also include policy essays, is that broad learning and talent for governing must reveal themselves here. This candidate's work in the first two sessions was certainly good, while his five policy essays cite historical precedents and address the actual circumstances precisely. This essay in particular offers proposals that are demonstrably practicable. How could one regard him as an ordinary bookish scholar? I had not expected …

title: 正德十一年湖廣鄉試錄
text:
奇偉之至於斯也
考試官教諭魏批區處湖南時務諸事而究
弊意成有歸非空言比也子即効用其必有可觀者
考試官教諭林批荆湖時弊所當為之謀者
莫此六事為急使老成諳練者窮日夜之思或未能
得其方畧而此於風簷寸晷之間乃能事事處置停
當若燭照數計而龜卜然雖未當盤根錯節之地而
利器之鋒芒已見矣楚材云乎哉
善治者必審弊以脩政知權者必因變以
===
===
為法夫政之弊有因變之生無定或出於
人或出於天而事機會于一時也故救弊
必有其策濟變必有其方其惟善治而知
變者能之乎苟弊而弗謀變而弗圖則民
病無瘳日而治且愈難矣執事軫荆湖之
民困於弊遭其變而明問及焉甚盛心也
敢不竭其愚以對且今日之荆湖即前日
之荆湖也不知安民治戎之政備邊救災
之策視前日果何如哉自我
punctuated:
奇偉之至於斯也！

考試官教諭魏批：區處湖南時務諸事，而究弊意成有歸，非空言比也。子即効用，其必有可觀者。

考試官教諭林批：荆湖時弊所當為之謀者，莫此六事為急。使老成諳練者窮日夜之思，或未能得其方畧，而此於風簷寸晷之間，乃能事事處置停當，若燭照數計而龜卜然。雖未當盤根錯節之地，而利器之鋒芒已見矣。楚材云乎哉！

善治者必審弊以脩政，知權者必因變以為法。夫政之弊有因，變之生無定，或出於人，或出於天，而事機會于一時也。故救弊必有其策，濟變必有其方，其惟善治而知變者能之乎！苟弊而弗謀，變而弗圖，則民病無瘳日，而治且愈難矣。執事軫荆湖之民困於弊、遭其變，而明問及焉，甚盛心也。敢不竭其愚以對？且今日之荆湖，即前日之荆湖也。不知安民治戎之政、備邊救災之策，視前日果何如哉？自我
translation_en:
…that such extraordinary excellence could reach this degree!

Comment by Examiner Wei, an Education Instructor: He arranges the various pressing affairs of Hunan and investigates their abuses, bringing his proposals to a definite conclusion [?]; this is no mere empty talk. If you enter service, you will surely have achievements worth seeing.

Comment by Examiner Lin, an Education Instructor: Among the current abuses in Jinghu that require remedies, none are more urgent than these six matters. Even seasoned and experienced men, exhausting their thoughts day and night, might fail to devise suitable strategies. Yet here, in the brief span allotted beneath the examination hall’s wind-swept eaves, he has managed to arrange every matter appropriately, with the clarity of illumination by a candle, the precision of counting, and the certainty of tortoise-shell divination. Although he has not yet confronted a situation of tangled roots and knotted joints, the keen edge of this fine instrument is already apparent. Here indeed is talent from Chu!

Those skilled in governing must examine abuses in order to improve administration; those who understand expediency must adapt to changing circumstances in establishing measures. Abuses in government have their causes, while changes arise unpredictably: some originate with people, others with Heaven, and the critical circumstances of affairs converge at a single moment. Thus, remedying abuses requires appropriate policies, and coping with changes requires appropriate methods. Surely only those skilled in governing and understanding change can accomplish this! If abuses are left without remedies and changes without plans, the people’s suffering will never be cured, and governing will become still more difficult. You, honored examiners, are concerned that the people of Jinghu suffer from abuses and encounter these upheavals, and have addressed them in your discerning question.
